content: The protein known as Acid-sensing ion channel 1 (ASIC1), also referred to as amiloride-sensitive cation channel 2, neuronal (ACCN2), or brain sodium channel 2 (BNaC2), is encoded by the ASIC1 gene in humans. This gene is one of five paralogous genes responsible for encoding proteins that assemble into trimeric acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs) in mammals. The cDNA corresponding to the ASIC1 gene was first cloned in 1996. The ASIC genes exhibit splicing variants, which result in the production of different protein isoforms. These genes are predominantly expressed in the central and peripheral nervous systems. ASICs are capable of forming both homotrimeric channels, which consist of three identical subunits, and heterotrimeric channels, which are composed of different subunits. The ASIC1 gene encodes a protein that belongs to the ASIC/ENaC superfamily. Members of this protein family are amiloride-sensitive sodium channels characterized by intracellular Nand C-termini, two hydrophobic transmembrane (TM) regions, and a large extracellular loop. The extracellular loop contains numerous cysteine residues with conserved spacing. The two transmembrane regions are typically referred to as TM1 (closer to the N-terminus) and TM2 (closer to the C-terminus). The ion-selective pore of the channel, which allows ions to flow from the extracellular space into the cytoplasm, is formed by the three TM2 regions of the trimeric structure. ASIC1 has been demonstrated to interact with the protein PICK1 (Protein Interacting with C Kinase 1).
